subject: Geography
board: National Curriculum (KS1-3), aligned to AQA GCSE 9-1
source: National Curriculum (KS2 geography: rivers, the water cycle, UK physical geography, human use of rivers) | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9): Tarbiyyah Primary Year 3 curriculum map and Geography Long Term Plan 2023-24 (Cornerstones Mighty Metals: rainforests); TGA Year 3 pack | Spring 2 2027: TGA Year 3 pack, History and geography, Tribal Tales (map skills and fieldwork)

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Rivers and the water cycle
lessons.title: The water cycle
objectives: Describe the four stages of the water cycle
Explain how water moves between the sea, the air and the land
Use key words: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection

keywords.def: when the sun heats water and turns it into water vapour
when water vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops of water
water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail
water gathering in rivers, lakes and seas
water as an invisible gas in the air

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four compass points.
What is a continent? Name one.
Where does rain come from? Write down what you think.

teach.heading: Water is always moving
bullets: The same water has been on Earth for millions of years.
It moves around in a never-ending cycle.
Allah says He made every living thing from water (Qur'an 21:30).
teach.note: Begin by showing a glass of water and asking: where has this water been before? Children may say a river or even a dinosaur's drink. The idea that water is recycled is surprising and exciting. The ayah is al-Anbiya 21:30: 'and We made from water every living thing'. Cite it plainly and move on.

teach.heading: Evaporation
bullets: The sun heats water in seas, rivers and puddles.
The water turns into water vapour, a gas.
The vapour rises into the air. We cannot see it.
teach.note: Demonstrate with a damp cloth in sunshine or a shallow dish of warm water. Ask where a puddle goes on a hot day. Misconception: children often think the water disappears or soaks into the ground. It rises into the air as an invisible gas.

teach.heading: Condensation and clouds
bullets: High up the air is cold.
Water vapour cools and turns into tiny drops.
Millions of drops join together to make clouds.
teach.note: Show a cold glass with droplets on the outside or a bathroom mirror that has steamed up. Ask where the droplets came from. They came from vapour in the air. Link to the cloud: the same thing happens high in the sky.

teach.heading: Precipitation and collection
bullets: When the drops get heavy they fall as rain.
Cold air can make snow, sleet or hail.
Water runs into rivers, then to lakes and seas.
teach.note: Draw the whole cycle on the board as a circle with arrows. Ask children to retell it using the four key words. Point out that rain on high land runs down into streams, then into rivers and finally the sea, where it can evaporate again.

teach.heading: The water cycle diagram
bullets: The cycle has no start or end.
The sun gives the energy to power the cycle.
teach.note: Show a labelled diagram and ask children to explain it in pairs, taking turns to be the water droplet 'telling its story'. Check for the language of sequence: first, next, then, finally. Notice who can explain why the cycle continues.

practice: Match each key word to its meaning: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection.
Put four pictures of the water cycle in the right order and say what is happening in each.
independent: Draw and label your own water cycle diagram with all four key words.
Write three sentences explaining what happens to a puddle on a sunny day.
Stretch: explain why rain falls from clouds, using the words condensation and precipitation.
lessons.homework: Put a little water in a clear cup, mark the level and leave it somewhere warm for two days. Write what you notice.
lessons.send: Provide a diagram with arrows already drawn and word cards to place. EAL: use picture cards for each stage. Stretch: ask why the cycle never runs out of water.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Rivers and the water cycle
lessons.title: The journey of a river
objectives: Name and describe the main features of a river
Describe the journey of a river from source to mouth
Explain how rivers change as they flow downhill

keywords.def: where a river begins, often high up in hills or mountains
a smaller river that joins a larger river
a bend or curve in a river
the place where a river meets the sea
the path the river water flows along

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four stages of the water cycle.
Where does the water in a river end up?

teach.heading: Where do rivers begin?
bullets: A river begins at its source.
The source is often high in hills or mountains.
Rain and springs feed the river.
teach.note: Link to the last lesson: precipitation falls on high ground and begins to flow downhill. Show a photograph of a small stream or spring on a hillside. Ask: why does water flow downhill? Because of gravity.

teach.heading: Flowing downhill
bullets: The river flows downhill towards the sea.
Small streams join to make bigger rivers.
A tributary is a smaller river joining a bigger one.
teach.note: Draw a tree-like picture of streams joining. Add the words tributary and confluence (where two rivers meet). Ask why a river gets wider as it goes. Many children think the river gets narrower when it is far from the source. The river grows because more water joins it.

teach.heading: Changes along the river
bullets: At the start it is narrow, steep and fast.
In the middle it widens and begins to bend.
Near the end it is wide, slow and flat.
teach.note: Show three photographs of one river: upper, middle and lower. Ask children to compare using adjectives. Introduce meanders as bends in the middle and lower parts of the river, where the land is flatter. Mention that rivers also pick up stones and soil and carry them downstream.

teach.heading: The mouth of the river
bullets: The mouth is where the river meets the sea.
Wide rivers often have an estuary at the mouth.
Fresh river water mixes with salty sea water.
teach.note: Show an aerial photo of an estuary. Estuary is a new word, so say it a few times. Ask what children think happens when fresh water meets salt water. Many creatures such as seabirds and fish feed in estuaries.

teach.heading: A river diagram
bullets: A diagram helps us follow the river's journey.
Use arrows to show the way the water flows.
teach.note: Model drawing and labelling a simple river diagram on the board. Check that the arrows point downstream. Ask a child to be the 'water drop' and describe the journey in the first person.

practice: Label a river diagram with source, tributary, meander and mouth.
Tell your partner: describe the river at the start and at the end.
independent: Draw a river from source to mouth and add five labels.
Write a short story called 'The journey of a raindrop' using at least four key words.
Stretch: explain why a river gets wider as it flows towards the sea.
lessons.homework: Find a river near you or in the news and write down its name and one fact about it.
lessons.send: Provide a partly labelled river diagram. EAL: use gestures for each term. Stretch: add the words confluence and estuary and explain their meaning.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Rivers and the water cycle
lessons.title: The River Thames
objectives: Locate the River Thames on a map of the UK
Describe the Thames from source to mouth
Name some important places on the Thames

keywords.def: the longest river in England, flowing through London
the wide part of a river where it meets the sea
a structure built to stop a river or sea flooding a city
a structure that lets people cross a river

starter: Say Bismillah. What is the source of a river?
Name the capital city of England.

teach.heading: The Thames on the map
bullets: The Thames is about 346 kilometres long.
It is the longest river that is only in England.
It flows east through London to the North Sea.
teach.note: Show a map of southern England with the Thames highlighted. The Severn is the longest river in the UK (about 354 km) but it flows through both Wales and England. Say 'the longest river entirely in England'. Ask children where the river begins and ends.

teach.heading: Source to mouth
bullets: The source is in Gloucestershire, in the Cotswolds.
It flows past Oxford, Reading, Windsor and London.
The mouth is the Thames Estuary at the North Sea.
teach.note: Use a simple route map. The usual source is at Thames Head near Kemble, though in dry weather the river may start further downstream. Point out how the river gets wider as it flows past each town. Ask: is the Thames wider in Oxford or in London? London.

teach.heading: London and the Thames
bullets: London grew up beside the Thames.
The Romans built a bridge here about 2,000 years ago.
Famous places: Tower Bridge, the London Eye, Big Ben.
teach.note: Show a photograph of the river through London. Ask why a city might grow next to a river (water for drinking, food, transport, trade). Many children in London will have crossed the river. Invite them to share a bridge they know.

teach.heading: Keeping London safe
bullets: The Thames is tidal in London. The sea pushes in.
It has gates that rise to stop floods.
teach.note: Explain that sea tides come up the river and a storm surge could flood parts of London. The Thames Barrier is a set of movable gates across the river at Woolwich. Show a photograph. Ask children what might happen if there were no barrier.

practice: On an outline map, trace the Thames from the Cotswolds to the North Sea.
Match these places to their pictures: Oxford, Windsor, London, Thames Barrier.
independent: Make a fact file about the River Thames with at least five facts.
Draw a map of the Thames and add three towns, the source and the mouth.
Stretch: explain two reasons why a big city grew beside a river.
exit: Is the Thames the longest river in the UK? Explain.
What does the Thames Barrier do?
lessons.homework: Draw your favourite bridge or landmark by a river and write two sentences about it.
lessons.send: Provide a fact-file template with sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach place names with photos. Stretch: compare the Thames with another river, such as the Nile.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Rivers and the water cycle
lessons.title: How people use rivers and stay safe
objectives: Describe different ways people use rivers
Explain why clean river water is important
Say how to stay safe near rivers and how to look after water

keywords.def: a large lake where water is stored for people to use
bringing water to crops to help them grow
something harmful added to air, land or water
moving people or goods from place to place

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two places the Thames flows through.
Where is the mouth of a river?
What do you use water for every day? List three things.

teach.heading: Why rivers matter
bullets: Rivers give us water to drink and wash with.
Farmers use river water for crops and animals.
People travel and carry goods by boat.
teach.note: Ask children to think about the last time they used water today. Point out that most tap water in the UK comes from rivers and reservoirs. Show photographs of a river boat, a farm and a water treatment works.

teach.heading: Rivers across the world
bullets: The River Nile flows through Egypt.
Farming in Egypt depends on the Nile.
Many cities and civilisations grew beside rivers.
teach.note: Show the Nile on a map. Egypt is mostly desert, so most people live close to the river. Ask children why. The Nile is one of the longest rivers on Earth (about 6,650 km). Check pupils' understanding with a quick map question.

teach.heading: Fun and energy from rivers
bullets: People fish, kayak and walk beside rivers.
Moving water can make electricity in hydroelectric dams.
Rivers are homes for fish, birds and plants.
teach.note: Link to the work on the water cycle: fast-moving water carries energy. A dam can use that energy to turn turbines. Ask which uses of rivers keep the river clean and which might harm it. Allow disagreement and reasons.

teach.heading: Keeping water clean
bullets: Polluted water can harm animals and people.
We must not waste water. Islam teaches us to avoid waste.
teach.note: Show photographs of a clean river and a polluted river. Ask: how can you tell? Link to stewardship: water is a blessing from Allah. Muslims are told not to be wasteful in eating and drinking (Qur'an 7:31). Invite children to suggest simple ways to save water at home, like turning off taps while brushing teeth.

teach.heading: Staying safe near water
bullets: Never go near a river alone.
Stay behind barriers and keep away from the edge.
Rivers can be cold, deep and fast.
teach.note: This is an important safety message. Many river drownings happen in summer because of cold water shock. Teach that if someone falls in, children should shout for help and call an adult, not jump in. Ask children to say a safety rule in their own words.

practice: Sort uses of rivers into: drinking, farming, travel, fun, energy.
Look at a photograph of a polluted river. Say two things that are wrong and one way to fix it.
independent: Make a poster: 'Look after our rivers' with three tips.
Write four sentences about how people use the River Nile or the Thames.
Stretch: explain how pollution in a river could harm people living far downstream.
exit: Give two ways people use rivers.
Give one rule for staying safe near water.
lessons.homework: Make a list of three ways your family could use less water this week and try one.
lessons.send: Provide sentence starters for the poster. EAL: use picture cards for uses of rivers. Stretch: ask pupils to evaluate whether dams are good or bad for people and nature.

lessons.title: Where are the rainforests?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do rainforests grow near the Equator and not in Britain?
objectives: To understand where the world's tropical rainforests are and why they grow there
successCriteria: All: find the Equator and the tropics on a world map
Most: locate the Amazon and Congo rainforests and their continents
Some: explain why rainforests grow between the tropics
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: plants need water, light and warmth
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at the variety of Allah's creation

keywords.def: a thick forest with a lot of rain all year
an imaginary line round the middle of the Earth
the hot area between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn
one of seven very large areas of land
the largest rainforest, in South America

hook.text: Which is easier to grow a jungle in: a hot wet place or a cold dry place? Why?

islamicLink.text: Allah sends the rain and brings plants out of the earth. Allah says He sends down water from the sky and with it brings out gardens full of beauty (an-Naml 27:60). The rainforests near the Equator show how much life Allah brings from rain.

starter.q: Which ocean is between Europe and North America?
Name the continent we live on.

teach.heading: Lines on the globe
bullets: The Equator goes round the middle
Tropic of Cancer is north of it
Tropic of Capricorn is south of it
teach.note: Show a globe or world map. Trace the Equator, then the two tropics. The area between is the tropics.

teach.heading: The world's rainforests
teach.note: Point to each on the map. All are near the Equator.

teach.heading: Why there?
bullets: The Sun is high all year: hot
Warm air rises and makes rain
Hot plus wet: plants grow fast
teach.note: Explain simply: near the Equator it is hot every day and it rains most days, so plants grow all year.

teach.heading: The Amazon
bullets: The River Amazon flows through it
teach.note: The Amazon covers parts of nine countries; most of it is in Brazil.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds, then share.

check.q: Which line do most rainforests lie close to?
check.why: Rainforests are in the hot, wet tropics near the Equator. The Arctic Circle is cold; the Prime Meridian runs north to south.

practice.q: Which continent is the Amazon rainforest in?
practice.model:
Find the Amazon on the map.
Look at the land around it.
It is in South America, mostly in Brazil.

practice.q: Which continent is the Congo rainforest in?
Is the UK in the tropics?
practice.a: No, it is far north of the Tropic of Cancer

independent.q: Core: On a blank world map, draw the Equator and the two tropics, then shade the Amazon and Congo rainforests.
independent.a: Equator across the middle, tropics either side; Amazon in northern South America, Congo in central Africa
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: a red line for the Equator through Brazil and Congo, dotted lines for the tropics, green shading for the rainforests.

independent.q: Extend: Label the continents your rainforests are on.
independent.a: South America and Africa (and Asia if Borneo is added)

independent.q: Stretch: Write one sentence: Rainforests grow near the Equator because ...
independent.a: ... it is hot and wet all year, so plants can grow all the time

exit.q: The Amazon is in:
exit.a: South America

exit.q: Big question: why do rainforests grow near the Equator and not in Britain?
exit.a: Near the Equator it is hot and rains a lot all year; Britain is too cold in winter and not wet enough all year

lessons.homework: Find three foods in your kitchen that may come from tropical countries and look up where they grow.
lessons.send: SEND: a map with the Equator already drawn and dots to shade. EAL: Equator, tropics, rainforest with pictures. Stretch: add the rainforests of South-East Asia.

lessons.title: The layers of the rainforest
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does each layer of the rainforest feel like a different world?
objectives: To understand how the rainforest is made of layers with different light and life
successCriteria: All: name the four layers in order
Most: describe the light and plants in each layer
Some: explain why the forest floor is dark
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah's care for every creature

keywords.def: the tallest trees that stick out above the rest
the thick roof of leaves
the dim layer of small trees and bushes
the dark ground at the bottom
one level on top of another

hook.text: If you climbed from the ground to the top of a rainforest tree, what would change as you went up?

islamicLink.text: Allah made every living thing in pairs and in its place. In the rainforest each layer has its own plants and animals, all looked after by Allah. Allah says there is no creature on earth except that Allah provides for it (Hud 11:6).

starter.q: Name the imaginary line round the middle of the Earth.

teach.heading: Four layers
teach.note: Draw four stacked boxes. Say them together from top to bottom.

teach.heading: Emergent and canopy
bullets: Emergent trees can grow over 50 m
teach.note: The canopy is like an umbrella. It catches most of the sunlight.

teach.heading: Understorey and forest floor
bullets: Plants have big leaves to catch light
teach.note: Ask: why might plants down here have huge leaves? To catch the little light there is.

teach.heading: Light in each layer
teach.note: Only a tiny part of the sunlight reaches the forest floor; use the chart as a picture of 'a lot' to 'very little'.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Which layer is the 'roof' of the rainforest?
check.why: The canopy is the thick roof of leaves. The understorey is below it and the forest floor is at the bottom.

practice.q: Put the layers in order from the top.
practice.model:
Start at the very top: emergent.
Then the roof of leaves: canopy.
Then the dim middle: understorey.
Last, the ground: forest floor.

practice.q: Which layer is darkest?
Where do most rainforest animals live?

independent.q: Core: Draw and label the four layers. Add one fact about each.
independent.a: Four labelled layers with facts such as: emergent, tallest trees; canopy, most animals; understorey, dim; forest floor, dark and leafy
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: draw the tall emergent tree, write 'emergent: tallest trees, over 50 m'.

independent.q: Extend: Add an arrow showing where the light comes from and how it gets less.
independent.a: An arrow from the top getting thinner towards the floor

independent.q: Stretch: Why do fallen leaves rot quickly on the forest floor?
independent.a: It is hot and wet, so tiny living things break them down fast

exit.q: The emergent layer is:
exit.a: The tallest trees

exit.q: Big question: why does each layer of the rainforest feel like a different world?
exit.a: Each layer gets a different amount of light, so different plants and animals live there

lessons.homework: Make a rainforest layers fold-out from a strip of paper folded into four.
lessons.send: SEND: layer labels to stick in the right boxes. EAL: top, middle, bottom, light, dark. Stretch: research one animal for each layer.

lessons.title: Rainforest climate and weather
lessons.bigQuestion: What would a week of weather be like in the Amazon?
objectives: To understand how the rainforest climate is hot, wet and humid all year
successCriteria: All: say that the rainforest is hot and wet
Most: read the rainfall for a month from a bar chart
Some: compare the rainforest climate with London's
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: rain as a sign of Allah

keywords.def: the usual weather of a place over many years
what it is like outside today
the air feels damp and sticky
how much rain falls
how hot or cold it is

hook.text: Would you rather live where it rains a little every day, or a lot in some months and hardly at all in others?

islamicLink.text: Allah drives the clouds and sends the rain. Allah says He sends the winds which stir up clouds, spreads them in the sky as He wills, and rain comes out of them (ar-Rum 30:48). The daily storms of the rainforest are this sign at work.

starter.q: What is the line round the middle of the Earth called?

teach.heading: Weather and climate
teach.note: Ask: is 'it is raining now' weather or climate? Weather.

teach.heading: Hot all year
bullets: The Sun is high near the Equator
teach.note: Manaus, a city in the middle of the Amazon, is about 27 °C in most months.

teach.heading: Wet all year
bullets: Over 2,000 mm of rain a year
teach.note: Rough monthly rain for Manaus (rounded). It is still wet in the 'dry' season compared with many places.

teach.heading: Humid
bullets: The air is full of water
teach.note: Trees give out water from their leaves, which rises and helps make more rain.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

options: The usual weather over many years
check.why: Climate is the usual pattern over many years; weather is what happens today.

practice.q: From the chart, how much rain falls in Manaus in March?
practice.model:
Find March on the bottom.
Go up to the top of the bar.
Read across: about 330 mm.

practice.q: Which month on the chart is driest?
London gets about 50 mm in a month. Is Manaus wetter or drier in March?

independent.q: Core: Write a weather report for a day in the Amazon. Use: hot, humid, rain, storm.
independent.a: For example: It is 27 °C and humid. In the afternoon there is a heavy storm.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Good morning from Manaus. It is already 26 °C and the air feels sticky. Heavy rain will fall this afternoon.'

independent.q: Extend: Give two differences between the Amazon climate and London's.
independent.a: The Amazon is hotter all year and much wetter; London has a cold winter

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why it rains so much in the rainforest.
independent.a: The hot sun makes warm wet air rise, it cools, makes clouds and heavy rain

exit.q: The rainforest climate is:
exit.a: Hot and wet all year

exit.q: Big question: what would a week of weather be like in the Amazon?
exit.a: Hot (about 27 °C), humid, with heavy rain or storms most days

lessons.homework: Keep a five-day weather diary at home and compare it with the Amazon.
lessons.send: SEND: a word mat for the report and a picture of a storm. EAL: hot, wet, humid, storm with pictures. Stretch: plot London's rainfall on the same chart.

lessons.title: Rainforest products and trade
lessons.bigQuestion: How did a rainforest tree end up in your bicycle tyres?
objectives: To understand how products from the rainforest are traded around the world
successCriteria: All: name three products that come from rainforests
Most: describe how a product travels from forest to shop
Some: explain how trade can be fair to farmers
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness to the people who grow our food

keywords.def: something made or grown to sell
something useful that people can use
a stretchy material made from the sap of a tree
buying and selling between places
trade that pays farmers a fair price

hook.text: Look around your kitchen. Could anything have started its life in a rainforest?

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches fair trade. Allah says: give full measure and weigh with an even balance (al-Isra 17:35). The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was a trusted trader known for his honesty. Paying farmers fairly for rainforest products follows this teaching.

starter.q: Where do most rainforest animals live?

teach.heading: Products from the forest
teach.note: Rubber trees and cocoa trees first grew in South America. Today most cocoa is grown in West Africa.

teach.heading: Rubber
teach.note: Tapping does not kill the tree, so it can be used for many years: a sustainable use.

teach.heading: From forest to shop
teach.note: Trace cocoa beans from a farm in Ghana to a shop in the UK on the map.

teach.heading: Fair trade
bullets: Farmers should get a fair price
Some products carry a Fairtrade mark
Fairness is part of good trade
teach.note: Ask: who does the hardest work? Who gets the most money? Is that fair?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: Rubber is made from latex, the white sap of the rubber tree.

practice.q: Put in order: ship, farm, shop, factory.
practice.model:
It starts where it grows: the farm.
Then it is made into the product: factory.
Then it travels: ship.
Last we buy it: shop.

practice.q: Name a product made from cocoa.
Why is tapping rubber trees a good way to use the forest?
practice.a: The trees stay alive and can be tapped for years

independent.q: Core: Make a flow chart showing how cocoa beans become a chocolate bar in a UK shop.
independent.a: Cocoa farm in West Africa, beans dried, factory makes chocolate, ship or lorry, UK shop
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: box 1 'cocoa pods picked on a farm in Ghana', arrow, box 2 'beans dried in the sun'.

independent.q: Extend: Add one product from a rainforest that you use at home.
independent.a: For example: a banana, a rubber ball, chocolate

independent.q: Stretch: Why is fair trade important for the farmer?
independent.a: So the farmer earns enough to feed their family for the hard work they do

exit.q: Which is a rainforest product?
exit.a: Cocoa

exit.q: Big question: how did a rainforest tree end up in your bicycle tyres?
exit.a: Sap from a rubber tree was collected, made into rubber in a factory and shipped to be made into tyres

lessons.homework: Look for the Fairtrade mark on three packets at home or in a shop and note what they are.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards of the four stages to order. EAL: farm, factory, ship, shop. Stretch: find which countries grow the most cocoa today.

lessons.title: Caring for the rainforest: stewards of the earth
lessons.bigQuestion: Should we stop cutting down rainforests, even if people need the land?
objectives: To understand why rainforests are cut down and how people can protect them
successCriteria: All: give two reasons why rainforests are cut down
Most: describe one effect of deforestation
Some: suggest how we can care for the rainforest as stewards
lessons.smsc: Moral: our duty as stewards of the earth

keywords.def: cutting down large areas of forest
protecting nature
someone who looks after something for its owner
raising cows on large farms
the home of an animal or plant

hook.text: If a farmer needs land to feed his family and the only land is forest, what should he do?

islamicLink.text: Allah says He made people successors (khulafa') on the earth (al-An'am 6:165), and that corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have done (ar-Rum 30:41). A Muslim is a steward: we may use the earth, but we must not waste or destroy it.

starter.q: Which layer is the roof of the forest?

starter.a: For example: cocoa, rubber, Brazil nuts

teach.heading: Why cut the forest?
bullets: Cattle ranching: the biggest cause in the Amazon
teach.note: People cut the forest to earn a living. That is why it is a hard problem.

teach.heading: What happens next?
bullets: Less carbon dioxide is soaked up

teach.heading: How we can care for it

check.q: What is the biggest cause of deforestation in the Amazon?
check.why: Clearing land for cattle is the biggest cause in the Amazon.

practice.q: Give one reason the rainforest is cut down.
practice.a: For example: land for cattle, farms or timber
practice.model:
Who wants the land?
Farmers want space for cows.
So one reason is cattle ranching.

practice.q: What happens to animals when their trees are cut?
practice.a: They lose their habitat and food

practice.q: Name one way to protect the rainforest.
practice.a: For example: national parks or planting trees

independent.q: Core: Write a short letter to a farmer explaining why the forest matters, using 'because'. Write in the portal response box or your book.
independent.a: For example: Please keep some forest because animals live there and it keeps the soil from washing away.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Dear farmer, I know you need land for your family. Please keep some trees because ...'

independent.q: Extend: Add one idea that helps the farmer and the forest.
independent.a: For example: grow crops under trees, collect Brazil nuts, or tap rubber

independent.q: Stretch: Is it fair to tell poor farmers not to cut trees? Give your view with a reason.
independent.a: For example: It is only fair if they get help to earn money another way

exit.q: A steward:
